svg.text: Goal: inspect data, compare species, and choose the right visual.
Choose each method to answer one clear data question.
Follow the arrows; each step prepares the next.
wide → long for one box plot
head() = first 5 rows • shape[0] = row count
Range is added manually; describe() omits it.
Compare each species separately, not all rows together.
A dict lets one feature use another rule: petal_length → max.
Exclude the categorical species label from numeric stats.
4. Pick a chart: histogram or scatter
Scatter = paired values for two numeric features.
Example: sepal length vs sepal width.
Seaborn combined box plot needs long-format data:
Petal length and width: strong upward relationship.
Labels, titles, figsize, alpha, and palette aid reading.
A reproducible workflow, then one fully grounded reshape example.
Wide data: one row holds several feature columns.
Pick the plot for the question; warnings are marked with [!].
• shape[0] = rows; columns = names; dtypes = types.
• describe() omits range; 50% is the median.
• Combined Seaborn boxplot requires long-format data.
• Figure = overall canvas; axes = individual plotting area.
• Overlaid histograms can hide one another; use alpha=0.5.
No factual conflict found between [S1] and [S2]. Summary flags likely transcript errors: “vegenica” → virginica; “medium” → median.
1. Inspect shape, columns, and types before analysis.
2. Summarize all data; group when species comparisons matter.
4. Box plots compare spread; pairplot surveys feature pairs.
5. Data shape matters: wide → long for the combined box plot.
[C] blue = concept • [P] green = process • [!] orange = caution
SOURCES: [S1] User-provided EDA summary • [S2] Uploaded IBM Machine Learning Foundation EDA Lab notebook
